meta.title: What is digital signage? A plain guide
meta.description: Digital signage explained without jargon: what it is, the three things you need, and what it costs. Written for people starting from zero.

hero.title: What is digital signage?
hero.subtitle: A screen that shows what you tell it to, and changes the moment you change your mind. This guide explains the whole thing from scratch — no jargon, no sales pitch.

sections.heading: The short answer
sections.body: Digital signage is a screen in a physical space that displays content you control remotely — a menu, a price list, an offer, a waiting-room notice, a departures board. The difference from a poster is that you change it from your phone in seconds instead of printing a new one. The difference from a television is that nobody has to touch it: it plays what you scheduled, on its own, all day.

sections.heading: Where you have already seen it
sections.body: The menu board above the counter at a fast-food chain. The screen in a pharmacy showing which number is being served. The board in a hotel lobby listing today's conference rooms. The window display in an estate agent's office that cycles through properties. All of it is the same three pieces doing the same job at different sizes.

sections.heading: The three things you need
sections.body: A screen, a player and software. The screen is usually a television you already own — any display with an HDMI input works. The player is a small device that plugs into it: an Android box the size of your hand, a mini-PC, or a computer already sitting nearby. The software is what you use to decide what plays and when, from a browser, anywhere. That is the entire shopping list.

sections.heading: What the player actually does
sections.body: It downloads your content, stores it locally and plays it in a loop. Storing it locally is the part that matters: when the internet drops, a player with a copy keeps going, while a player that streams shows a blank screen or an error to everyone walking past. Ask about this before you buy anything — it is the single most common way a signage setup embarrasses its owner.

sections.heading: What it costs
sections.body: Three separate numbers, and vendors tend to blur them. The screen you probably own. The player is a one-off purchase, typically between €50 and €200 depending on whether you need a cheap Android box or a mini-PC that runs sixteen hours a day. The software is a monthly subscription per screen — the market sits between €8 and €45, and the range mostly reflects how much a vendor holds back for higher plans. SignageWall is {price} per screen with everything included.

sections.heading: How long it takes to set up
sections.body: The first screen takes minutes, not days. Plug the player into the screen and the mains, install the app, scan the code that appears, and it is paired to your account. Building the first piece of content — a menu, a price list, a welcome message — usually takes longer than the pairing does. Every screen after the first is faster, because the content already exists and you are just pointing it at a new device.

sections.heading: What to put on the screen
sections.body: Less than you think. A screen that tries to say six things says none of them: a passer-by gives it a second or two. Pick one message per slide, make the text large enough to read from where people actually stand, and let the schedule do the work — breakfast in the morning, lunch at noon, the evening list at six. The most effective screens are the ones that change with the day rather than the ones with the most on them.

sections.heading: How to tell whether it is working
sections.body: A screen has no click-through rate, but it is not unmeasurable. Track the sales of the item you feature and compare it to the weeks before. Count how often staff get asked the question the screen was meant to answer. If a screen is showing a QR code, the scans are countable directly. Pick one number before you start, so you are not deciding after the fact whether it worked.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.body: Pushing the same content to every screen in a building, when the customer at the window and the customer in the queue are thinking about different things. Text sized for a designer's monitor rather than for four meters away. A static logo burnt into the corner of a panel after a year. Buying a professional display when an ordinary television would have lasted years, or the reverse — an ordinary television in a sunlit window, where it will never be bright enough.

sections.heading: Where to go next
sections.body: If you want to see what it looks like for your kind of business, the solutions pages walk through specific setups by industry. If you want the numbers, the pricing page has them without a sales call. If you would rather just try it, a trial takes a few minutes and needs no card.

items.q: Is digital signage the same as a smart TV?
items.a: No. A smart TV plays what somebody selects on it. Digital signage plays what you scheduled from somewhere else, restarts itself after a power cut, and keeps going without anyone touching the remote. You can run signage on a smart TV, but the software is what makes it signage.

items.q: Do I need a special screen?
items.a: Usually not. An ordinary television is fine for normal hours indoors. Purpose-built displays are brighter, built for sixteen-hour days, and often come in portrait — worth it for a sunlit window or a screen that never turns off, unnecessary for a café wall.

items.q: Does it need to be connected all the time?
items.a: It needs a connection to receive new content, not to play it. Good signage software downloads and stores content locally, so the screen keeps working through an outage and catches up when the connection returns.

items.q: How many screens do I need to make it worthwhile?
items.a: One. A single screen above a counter replaces a printed price list you were reprinting anyway. The economics get better with more screens because the content is already made, but there is no threshold you have to cross.

items.q: Can I use it for a shop window?
items.a: Yes, with the right display. A window screen competes with daylight, so it needs to be much brighter than an indoor one, and it should power down overnight unless there is foot traffic. The software is the same.

items.q: What if I have no designer?
items.a: Most platforms, including ours, ship ready-made layouts you fill in with your own text and prices. For a menu or a price list you do not need a designer at all — you need consistent type and enough contrast.
